original_value: Subjective experience of human control over remote, artificial, or virtual limbs has traditionally been investigated from two separate angles: presence research originates from teleoperation, aiming to capture to what extent the user feels like actually being in the remote or virtual environment. Embodiment captures to what extent a virtual or artificial limb is perceived as one’s own limb. Unfortunately, the two research fields have not interacted much. This survey intends to provide a coherent overview of the literature at the intersection of these two fields to further that interaction. Two rounds of systematic research in topic-related data bases resulted in 414 related articles, 14 of which satisfy the deliberately strict inclusion criteria: 2 theoretical frameworks that highlighted intersections and 12 experimental studies that evaluated subjective measures for both concepts. Considering the surrounding literature as well, theoretical and experimental potential of embodiment and presence are discussed and suggestions to apply them in teleoperation research are derived. While increased publication activity is observed between 2016 and 2018, potentially caused by affordable virtual reality technologies, various open questions remain. To tackle them, human-in-the-loop experiments and three guiding principles for teleoperation system design (mechanical fidelity, spatial bodily awareness, and self-identification) are suggested.

result.paraphrase: The subjective experience of human control over remote, artificial, or virtual limbs has traditionally been studied from two distinct perspectives. Presence research, which emerged from teleoperation, seeks to determine how much the user feels truly present in the remote or virtual environment. Embodiment examines how much a virtual or artificial limb is experienced as one’s own. However, these two research areas have interacted only minimally. This survey aims to offer a unified overview of the literature at their intersection and thereby encourage greater interaction. Two rounds of systematic searches in topic-related databases yielded 414 relevant articles, of which 14 met the intentionally strict inclusion criteria: 2 theoretical frameworks highlighting the overlap and 12 experimental studies assessing subjective measures of both concepts. In light of the broader literature, the theoretical and experimental potential of embodiment and presence is discussed, and recommendations for applying them in teleoperation research are derived. Although publication activity increased between 2016 and 2018, possibly due to affordable virtual reality technologies, several open questions remain. To address them, human-in-the-loop experiments and three guiding principles for teleoperation system design—mechanical fidelity, spatial bodily awareness, and self-identification—are proposed.
